content: Palmitic acid, also known as hexadecanoic acid in IUPAC nomenclature, is one of the most prevalent saturated fatty acids found in both animals and plants. As its name suggests, it is a significant component of palm oil and palm kernel oil, which are derived from palm trees. The term palmitic originates from the French word palmitique, referring to the pith of the palm tree. This fatty acid is also present in various animal-derived products such as butter, cheese, milk, and meat. The term palmitate refers to the salts or esters of palmitic acid. At physiological pH, palmitic acid exists predominantly in its anionic form, known as the palmitate anion. In biochemistry, palmitic acid is the first fatty acid synthesized during lipogenesis (fatty acid synthesis). It serves as the precursor for the production of longer fatty acids. Palmitate exerts a negative feedback effect on acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC), an enzyme responsible for converting acetyl-ACP to malonyl-ACP during the elongation of the acyl chain. This feedback mechanism inhibits further production of palmitate. Additionally, the reduction of palmitic acid results in the formation of cetyl alcohol. Palmitate has several applications. It functions as an antioxidant and is used as a vitamin A compound in low-fat milk to restore the vitamin content lost during the removal of milk fat. Specifically, palmitate is attached to the alcohol form of vitamin A, retinol, to stabilize vitamin A in milk. During World War II, derivatives of palmitic acid were combined with naphtha to produce napalm, a mixture of naphthenic and palmitic acids. The World Health Organization (WHO) has reported convincing evidence that dietary intake of palmitic acid increases the risk of developing cardiovascular diseases. However, other studies, which may be less impartial, have shown no adverse effects—or even beneficial effects—of dietary palmitic acid on blood lipids and cardiovascular health. This discrepancy renders the WHO's findings somewhat controversial. It has been suggested that palmitic acid consumption may be acceptable if it constitutes no more than 5% of total energy intake. However, if the diet also includes trans fatty acids, the health effects could be detrimental, leading to an increase in LDL cholesterol and a decrease in HDL cholesterol.
